item.title: Traumatic Left Main Coronary Artery-Left Anterior Descending Artery Dissection in an Adolescent: A Case Report
item.description:
Background: In adolescents with high-energy blunt chest trauma, electrocardiography (ECG) findings suggestive of myocardial infarction together with markedly elevated cardiac enzymes should raise immediate suspicion for traumatic coronary artery dissection (TCAD).

Case report: We report the case of a 16-year-old male who sustained blunt chest trauma in an electric bicycle accident. During venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) support, non-ECG-gated contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography (CT) was performed. Thin-slice (1.25 mm) delayed-phase images incidentally revealed a double-lumen sign from the left main coronary artery to the proximal left anterior descending artery, along with diffuse myocardial hypoperfusion. These findings prompted angiographic confirmation and urgent coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). WHY SHOULD AN EMERGENCY PHYSICIAN BE AWARE OF THIS?: This case highlights that, in hemodynamically unstable trauma patients, when ECG-gated coronary computed tomography angiography (CTA) is not feasible, careful evaluation of routinely obtained contrast-enhanced CT images, particularly coronary root morphology and myocardial perfusion, may provide critical diagnostic clues to this life-threatening condition.

Xu K, Xu N, Liu W, Zhu X, Xu Y

item.title: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Intranasal Opioids vs. Intravenous Morphine for Acute Moderate-to-Severe Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
item.description:
Background: Intranasal (IN) opioids may provide noninvasive analgesia without delays associated with intravenous (IV) access, but their efficacy and safety vs. IV morphine remain uncertain.

Objectives: To synthesize randomized evidence comparing IN opioids with IV morphine for acute moderate-to-severe pain.

Methods: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to May 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in adults or children with acute moderate-to-severe pain in emergency, prehospital, procedural, or postoperative settings. Eligible trials directly compared IN opioids with IV morphine. The primary outcome was change in pain score from baseline at 20 and 30 minutes. Secondary outcomes included rescue analgesia and adverse events. Outcomes were pooled as standardized mean differences (SMD) or risk ratios (RR) using random-effects models.

Results: Ten RCTs involving 1164 participants were included. IN opioids showed comparable analgesic efficacy to IV morphine at 20 minutes (SMD = -0.05, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.24 to 0.14; p = 0.59; I² = 11.94%) and 30 minutes (SMD = -0.05, 95% CI: -0.24 to 0.15; p = 0.64; I² = 0.00%). Rescue analgesia was comparable (RR = 1.00, 95% CI: 0.81-1.25; p = 0.98). No significant differences were observed in overall adverse events, serious adverse events, respiratory complications, hypotension, gastrointestinal events, dizziness, or rhinorrhea. Dysgeusia was borderline increased.

Conclusion: IN opioids provide analgesic efficacy comparable to IV morphine at 20 and 30 minutes, with no clear increase in systemic adverse events. Larger trials should confirm safety for rare serious events and optimize dosing.

Fida L, Alahmed H, Almutairi AS, AlNassar SY, Alanazi SA, Martan R

item.title: Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection: An Emergency Medicine-Focused Narrative Review
item.description:
Background: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is a nontraumatic, noniatrogenic dissection of a coronary artery.

Objective: This narrative review provides emergency clinicians with a focused overview of the presentation, evaluation, and management of SCAD.

Discussion: SCAD is an underrecognized and potentially deadly disease that can result in coronary artery occlusion and acute coronary syndrome (ACS). It traditionally affects young-to-middle aged females, with increased risk in the peripartum period. Patients with SCAD most commonly present with signs and symptoms consistent with ACS, and a significant proportion of patients will have ST elevation myocardial infarction on electrocardiogram. Emergent cardiology consultation for angiography is necessary for diagnosis. Following diagnosis, a conservative approach is often followed, as most lesions heal spontaneously without intervention. Revascularization in the form of percutaneous coronary artery intervention or coronary artery bypass grafting is necessary in those with ongoing or recurrent ischemia with electrocardiogram or troponin changes, hemodynamic instability, ventricular dysrhythmias, or dissection of the left main coronary artery. Patients can have recurrence of SCAD, and noninvasive imaging modalities, such as coronary computed tomography, may be considered to diagnose recurrence.

Conclusions: Emergency physicians should consider SCAD in patients presenting with ACS, particularly younger women and those without traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Early recognition and prompt consultation with cardiology to guide selection of conservative vs. revascularization strategies are essential to optimize patient outcomes.

item.title: The Omokhodion Method: A High-Success, Low-Force Technique for Shoulder Dislocations
item.description:
Background: Shoulder dislocation is a common emergency presentation, and reduction may be complicated by pain, involuntary muscle guarding, patient positioning, clinician experience, associated injury, and the need for analgesia or procedural sedation. Because no single reduction maneuver is optimal for every patient or clinical setting, emergency physicians benefit from having multiple safe, reproducible, low-force techniques available.

Clinical problem: Many established reduction methods rely to varying degrees on traction, leverage, sustained positioning, or sequential rotation. Although these approaches may be effective, escalating force can worsen pain and protective muscular contraction in some patients, making reduction more difficult.

Technique: This technical report describes the Omokhodion method, a standardized low-force shoulder reduction technique based on upright positioning when feasible, continuous two-point support of the affected extremity, maintenance of approximately 90° of elbow flexion, supported abduction, controlled external rotation, gradual adduction toward the ipsilateral hip, and final internal rotation across the abdomen. Movement is performed slowly within the patient's tolerated range, and progression is paused when pain or guarding increases. Forceful longitudinal traction and abrupt leverage are avoided.

Discussion: The proposed biomechanical rationale is that continuous limb support, controlled positioning, progressive soft-tissue accommodation, and deliberate pacing may reduce gravitational loading and counterproductive muscle guarding while facilitating restoration of glenohumeral alignment. The method is intended to complement, not replace, established shoulder reduction techniques, and standard principles of neurovascular assessment, analgesia, procedural sedation, imaging, immobilization, and orthopedic consultation remain applicable.

Conclusion: The Omokhodion method provides a structured and reproducible low-force option for shoulder dislocation reduction and procedural education. Prospective clinical and biomechanical studies are needed to define its effectiveness, safety, optimal indications, reproducibility, and comparative performance relative to established reduction techniques.

item.title: Changes in Antiviral Treatment for Hospitalized Adults with Influenza in United States Emergency Departments
item.description:
Background: Early administration of an antiviral reduces influenza-related complications, and multiple guidelines recommend prompt antiviral treatment for all hospitalized patients with influenza. However, there is limited data on early antiviral treatment within the Emergency Department (ED).

Study objectives: Our epidemiological study assesses temporal trends in the initiation of antiviral treatment for adults hospitalized with influenza in the ED and identifies factors associated with nonadherence.

Methods: This retrospective cohort study examined antiviral treatment patterns among adults hospitalized with influenza in a U.S. ED from 2016 to 2025, using Epic Cosmos. Patients with ICD-10-coded or laboratory-confirmed influenza A/B were included. The primary outcome was the proportion of hospitalized patients who received oseltamivir, peramivir, baloxavir, or zanamivir in the ED.

Results: Of the 483,459 hospitalized ED patients with influenza, 416,982 (86.25%) received an antiviral in the ED. Antiviral treatment ranged from 72.7% in 2021 to 91.08% in 2020, rebounding to 85.11% in 2025. Differences in demographics between treated and untreated patients were observed across age, ethnicity, race, and spoken language. The likelihood of antiviral therapy was lower in the South (odds ratios [OR] 0.95; 95% confidence intervals [CI] 0.93-0.97) and West (OR 0.78; 95% CI 0.76-0.80) compared to the Northeast of the United States. The rate of antiviral treatment was moderately correlated with the national rate of influenza positivity in the ED (Pearson correlation 0.59).

Conclusion: Although prompt administration of an antiviral for hospitalized patients reduces influenza-related complications, antiviral administration is not universal in the ED. Our study highlights a critical gap that requires urgent implementation of mitigation strategies.

Buell KG, Vahora R, Le KN, Kim JY, Moyer E, Bernard K

item.title: Predictors of Technical Difficulty in Emergency Department Ultrasound-Guided Nerve Blocks: A Multicenter NURVE Registry Analysis
item.description:
Background: Ultrasound-guided nerve blocks (UGNBs) are increasingly used in emergency departments (EDs), but factors associated with technical difficulty remain poorly characterized.

Objectives: To characterize the frequency of technical difficulty during ED UGNBs and explore patient-, provider-, and block-level factors associated with difficult procedures.

Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of the multicenter National Ultrasound-guided neRVE (NURVE) Registry, including UGNBs performed at 11 U.S. EDs from January 2022 through December 2023. This interval was selected to capture the complete initial two-year period of NURVE Registry data collection. Technical difficulty was defined by operator self-report using a standardized registry question. Mixed-effects logistic regression with institution as a random intercept was used to evaluate factors associated with technical difficulty.

Results: Among 1725 UGNBs included in the analysis, 82 (4.8%) were reported as technically difficult. In unadjusted analyses, technical difficulty was more common among patients with obesity and differed by block group. In mixed-effects regression, body mass index (BMI) ≥ 30 kg/m² was independently associated with increased odds of technical difficulty compared with BMI 18.5-24.9 kg/m² (odds ratio [OR] 2.94, 95% confidence intervals [CI] 1.58-5.47). Compared with fascia iliaca/femoral region blocks, truncal plane blocks (OR 0.20, 95% CI 0.05-0.87), distal upper-extremity blocks (OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02-0.94), and distal lower-extremity blocks (OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.10-0.99) were associated with lower odds of technical difficulty. Provider role and prior procedural experience were not significantly associated with difficulty in unadjusted analyses.

Conclusions: Technical difficulty during ED UGNBs was uncommon. Obesity was the most consistent predictor of procedural difficulty, while block-group associations were more modest and influenced by site-level factors. These findings may help inform procedural planning and UGNB training initiatives.

Driver L, Perice L, Rizvi TZ, Duggan NM, Riscinti M, Martin D

item.title: Developing a Model for Hospital Staff Preparedness in Patient Evacuation During Disasters: A Mixed-Methods Study
item.description:
Background: Hospital staff preparedness for patient evacuation during disasters is a component of healthcare resilience. Current protocols may lack evidence-based foundations and tend to rely on static, checklist-driven approaches. Competency-based models have been proposed as an alternative, but empirical evidence supporting their effectiveness is limited.

Objectives: This study aimed to develop a model for hospital evacuation readiness, grounded in global evidence and local expertise.

Methods: An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was conducted in Iran (2023-2025) across five phases: 1) systematic review; 2) qualitative interviews with hospital staff; 3) data integration and expert refinement using a Modified Nominal Group Technique; 4) Delphi consensus validation with specialists; and 5) final model design. The model was developed as a theoretical framework; empirical testing of its effectiveness was beyond the study's scope.

Results: Of 52 initially identified components, 50 were validated through Delphi consensus. The framework identifies five domains: individual factors; education and empowerment; resources; evacuation processes; and communication and coordination. The model introduces practical elements such as stress-tested drills, preemptive resource mapping, and structured near-miss learning.

Conclusions: This research proposes a reconceptualization of evacuation preparedness as an evolving, competency-driven system. The framework offers hospitals strategies to strengthen training, optimize resources, and institutionalize near-miss learning. However, its effectiveness compared with static approaches remains theoretical and requires longitudinal empirical evaluation. Hospitals in resource-constrained regions may particularly benefit from its emphasis on adaptive capacity and low-cost, simulation-based training.

Moslehi S, Tavan A, Ajri-Khameslou M, Dadkhah B, Narimani S
